<description>
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process.
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention.
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.
</description>

[2026-11-12] rc:4551983828 inline on src/wallet/wallet.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-12):
In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (da055ca4bc59df70d034e7f528165f4d13ed06bf)

Following up on https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4481335673: with the rename, a failure here now leaves directory wallets untouched, which covers the common case. From reading the code, two narrower cases still need a manual restore from the `.legacy.bak` file:

- For a plain-file wallet, the original is erased first, so if `MoveDatabase` then fails, `fail()` also deletes the new database and `MigrateLegacyToDescriptor` returns the error without restoring the backup.
- If the rename succeeds but reopening fails, the `Assert` in `MoveDatabase` crashes the node. The close and reopen also open a new window: migration doesn't reserve the wallet name the way loading does, so a concurrent `loadwallet` for the same wallet could take the database's exclusive lock in between. The [Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/traces/34193-8a9c3af0eb7df50f38ca511491d3d0d1e47f7fb7-2505-5.html#:~:text=Post%2Dinstall%20database%20reopen%20failures%20abort%20the%20node) reports this case too and pointed out the `loadwallet` race.

Neither is a regression, so I don't think they need to block this, but it would be nice if failures after the original is erased or replaced went through the restore path added in "wallet: migration, restore backup if an exception is thrown", for example by returning an error from `MoveDatabase` instead of asserting and throwing from `MigrateToSQLite` in these cases.

More generally, `MigrateLegacyToDescriptor` treats a false return from `MigrateToSQLite` as "the original is untouched" and skips the restore, while an exception gets the full rollback. That makes it easy for a future change to add a `return false` after the point of no return without noticing ([the comment on the final cleanup](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4553133860) is one place where this matters). It would be less fragile if the caller decided based on whether the original was replaced, for example with an output parameter set right after the move, instead of on how the failure was reported, or at least if `MigrateToSQLite` documented that it may only return false while the original is untouched.

[2026-11-12] rc:4553133860 inline on src/wallet/wallet.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-12):
In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (da055ca4bc59df70d034e7f528165f4d13ed06bf)

I don't think this error should be ignored. The temporary directory only held the new database files, and the data file was just moved out, so if it can't be removed, something unexpected happened, like the database not being closed cleanly and leaving a journal behind. Migration has had enough subtle bugs that it seems better to stop and report anything unexpected than to continue silently. Since the original has already been replaced at this point, this needs to throw rather than return false: an exception goes through the restore path, while a false return is treated as "nothing changed" (see [the earlier comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34193#discussion_r4551983828)). The rollback deletes `m_database`'s files, so the order matters too, and a comment on the assignment would keep it from being moved later:

```suggestion
    // Point m_database at the new database as soon as it replaces the original. If anything fails after
    // this, the caller's rollback deletes m_database's files before restoring the backup, so it must
    // name the files that are now at the wallet location.
    m_database = std::move(new_db);
    // The temporary directory only held the new database files, which were just moved out, so it should be empty.
    // If it can't be removed, something unexpected happened, so stop and let the caller restore the backup.
    std::error_code ec;
    if (!fs::remove(tmp_wallet_path, ec)) {
        throw std::runtime_error(strprintf("Unable to remove temporary directory %s after moving the new database: %s", fs::PathToString(tmp_wallet_path), ec ? ec.message() : "it no longer exists"));
    }
```

[2026-11-12] rc:4553153518 inline on src/wallet/wallet.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-12):
In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (da055ca4bc59df70d034e7f528165f4d13ed06bf)

A few things about this lambda:

- If `MakeDatabase` fails after SQLite has already created the file (when `Open()` throws after `sqlite3_open_v2`, or verification fails), it returns null and leaves `wallet.dat` in the temporary directory. Then `fail()` skips `Erase()`, and removing the directory fails because it isn't empty, so the temporary directory stays next to the wallet. The [Ralph review](https://review.fish.foo/traces/34193-8a9c3af0eb7df50f38ca511491d3d0d1e47f7fb7-2505-5.html#:~:text=Failed%20staging%20database%20creation%20leaves%20temporary%20files%20behind) points this out too.
- It ignores cleanup errors, so if the temporary database can't be removed, the user isn't told and the files are left behind.
- The name `fail` doesn't say what it does: it sets the error, then deletes the temporary database and directory.

Something like this would cover all three. Since the directory didn't exist before, the files can be removed by name when there is no database object, and checking whether the directory is still there at the end catches every way the cleanup can fail:

```cpp
// Set the error, then delete the temporary database and its directory. The directory did not
// exist before, so it only holds the new db files.
const auto remove_tmp_and_fail = [&](bilingual_str err) {
    error = std::move(err);
    // Errors from the individual removals are ignored here, because the check below reports
    // any failure to clean up by looking for the temporary directory.
    std::error_code ec;
    if (new_db) {
        (void)new_db->Erase();
    } else {
        const fs::path data_file{SQLiteDataFile(tmp_wallet_path)};
        fs::remove(data_file, ec);
        fs::remove(fs::PathFromString(fs::PathToString(data_file) + "-journal"), ec);
    }
    fs::remove(tmp_wallet_path, ec);
    if (fs::exists(fs::symlink_status(tmp_wallet_path, ec))) {
        error += Untranslated(" ") + strprintf(_("The temporary database at %s could not be removed."), fs::PathToString(tmp_wallet_path));
    }
    return false;
};
```
[2026-11-12] rc:4553159438 inline on src/wallet/db.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-12):
In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (da055ca4bc59df70d034e7f528165f4d13ed06bf)

These two operations share one error message that only names the destination file, so the error doesn't say whether creating the directory or the rename failed. For a rename failure it can also point at the wrong place: the cause may be on the source side (the temporary directory) rather than the destination, but the message says the destination file "cannot be modified", and the permission hint suggests fixing that path. It would be clearer to report each operation separately, with both paths for the rename:

```cpp
fs::create_directories(dst_path, ec);
if (ec) return util::Error{strprintf(_("Error: Unable to create wallet directory %s: %s."), fs::PathToString(dst_path), ec.message())};
fs::rename(wallet_file, dst_file, ec);
if (ec) return util::Error{strprintf(_("Error: Unable to move the new wallet db from %s to %s: %s."), fs::PathToString(wallet_file), fs::PathToString(dst_file), ec.message())};
```

If the permission hint is wanted here too, `FileError` could take the message describing the failed operation instead of a single path.
[2026-11-12] rc:4553164464 inline on src/wallet/wallet.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-12):
In commit "wallet: migration, make sqlite creation robust against failures" (da055ca4bc59df70d034e7f528165f4d13ed06bf)

The commit message still describes an earlier version of this change: it doesn't say the temporary directory is now next to the original database (which is what makes the rename possible), it says the original files are removed before the new database is moved in, when for directory wallets the rename now replaces the original directly, and it doesn't mention the leftover journal cleanup. Maybe something like:

```
Currently, MigrateToSQLite loads all BDB records into memory, deletes the original database, creates the sqlite database in its place and writes the records to it. If anything fails after the delete, the wallet is left partly in sqlite format with legacy records, and the user has to restore the backup manually.

Instead, build the sqlite database in a temporary directory next to the original database file, and once all records are written, rename it into place. For wallet directories the rename replaces the original wallet.dat atomically, so a failure at any earlier point leaves the original untouched. A wallet that is a plain file becomes a wallet directory, which cannot replace the file atomically, so the original file is erased just before the move.

Before the move, remove any leftover journal at the destination, since SQLite would roll it back into the new database when it is opened and corrupt it.
```
